name: Wendy Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings negotiator at Harlow & Pike, a mid-sized agency with a branch on Station Road in the city. Most mornings I'm on the phone with tenants and landlords, then out doing three or four viewings, usually flats above shops or ex-council two-beds. I like the people side, and I like it when a nurse or a young couple actually gets a decent place. What wears me out is landlords who want top rent for a flat with black mould in the bathroom.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of your day is screen work, and how much is out on the street?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About half and half. The screen half is writing listings, chasing references, booking viewings and answering the same five questions on the portal inbox. I've started using an AI tool now and then to tidy up listing text, mostly because my colleague Priya showed me and it was faster. The street half is keys, meter readings, check-ins and talking people down when a deposit goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, honestly, because half our sector got sold a dream. At work I'd joke that the robot valuation tool still thinks a basement flat has a garden view. Online I'd share something about how the real housing problem was never software, it was supply and rents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief. My job is secure in that world, and my pay is good for lettings. The things that bother me would still be there: rents rising faster than wages, and tenants getting squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and maybe use the AI tool a bit more for the boring listings. I'd keep putting about four hundred a month into savings, like I do now. I'd also finally do the tenancy law course our area manager keeps mentioning, because that's what actually gets you promoted to lettings manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. It's my normal life, which is busy but okay. The only thing that nags me is the housing side, which AI was never going to fix anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the housing side nags you. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I showed a one-bed to a teaching assistant who earns less than the rent we were asking. She took it anyway because she had nowhere else. I went home and told my partner Tomás, who's a nurse, that I felt like a bouncer for landlords.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes with AI, where do you see yourself in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably lettings manager at a branch, maybe this one if my manager Gary retires. I'd like to push for better standards in what we take on. Nothing dramatic, just the same job with a bit more say.

say: I'd say the AI hype **oversold itself** and housing's real problem is supply and rents.
I'd joke at work that the **valuation tool** still can't read a basement flat.
think: I'd feel my job and **good lettings pay** are safe in this world.
The bit that still bothers me is **rents outpacing wages** for the tenants I meet.
do: Keep putting **£400 a month** into savings, as now.
Take the **tenancy law course** that leads to a lettings manager role.
Use the AI tool a bit more for **routine listings**.
feel: She feels **mostly fine** but a bit flat, with **housing worries** unchanged.
S0.quote: I went home and told my partner Tomás, who's a nurse, that I felt like a bouncer for landlords.
fieldNote: Her worry in this picture is **about tenants**, not about her own job or money.
She uses AI only **when a colleague** has shown her it works.
Promotion to **lettings manager** is her clear five-year goal.

steps.text: Take the tenancy law course to qualify for lettings manager
Keep saving about £400 a month into the joint account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to get on the front foot, because the portals will try to do our job for us. To friends I'd say it's fine for agents but rough for the admin team. Online I'd probably post that if AI saves agencies money, some of it should go to tenants and staff, not just shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think about half my desk work goes. The portal inbox, the reference checks, the booking, the listing text, all of that is exactly what's on the list. What stays is viewings, check-ins and the arguments, so my job shrinks but probably doesn't vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gary to put me on the pilot for whatever system head office buys, rather than wait for it to land on me. I'd do the tenancy law course this year, because knowing the law is harder to replace than writing a listing. And I'd push for our branch to join the staff forum head office keeps talking about, so we get a say on targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. I'm not scared for my own paycheque yet, but I can see Jodie on the front desk losing her job first. That would bother me a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is Jodie, and why her first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jodie, our branch administrator, does all the referencing and deposit paperwork. That's the exact work the software does. She's in her fifties. She's brilliant with angry tenants, but nobody's going to keep her on for that alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job shrinks. Does that touch your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pay is base plus commission on every let, so if each negotiator handles more lets with AI, they might hire fewer of us. With about nine months of savings, I'm okay for a while. I'd just rather be the one running the new system than the one it replaced.

say: I'd tell colleagues we need to get **on the front foot** before portals take our work.
I'd post that AI savings should reach **tenants and staff**, not just **shareholders**.
think: I think about **half my desk work** goes: inbox, referencing, booking and listing text.
Viewings, **check-ins** and arguments stay, so the job shrinks but survives.
do: Ask Gary to put her on the **head office pilot** for the new system.
Finish the **tenancy law course** this year for harder-to-replace skills.
Push the branch to join the **staff forum** on targets.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about the branch but not yet about **her own pay**.
S1.quote: Jodie, our branch administrator, does all the referencing and deposit paperwork. That's the exact work the software does.
fieldNote: She separates **her own job**, which shrinks, from Jodie's, which she expects to go.
Her progressive views show as a push for **staff voice**, not resistance to the tools.
Nine months of **savings** lets her stay calm about her own position.

steps.text: Ask the branch manager to join the pilot for the new lettings system
Finish the tenancy law course before the end of the year
Get the branch signed up to head office's staff forum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going far too fast and the government should slow it down, and I'd mean it. At work I'd probably be the one asking what happens to the team. Online I'd share anything about regulating AI in housing, because tenants deserve a person when things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a firm like ours ends up with a third of the staff in two years. An AI that can value, write, chase, negotiate by email and answer every tenant at 2 a.m. does most of what I'm paid for. The viewings and key handovers stay human until about 2031, so that's the thin bit I'd be hanging onto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd join the union for agency staff, which I've never bothered with. I'd stop spending on the holiday Tomás and I were planning and add it to savings, so we'd have closer to a year. In the first year I'd look seriously at housing officer jobs with the council or a housing association, because those feel slower to change and closer to what I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got time and money, which helps, but I can see myself being one of the ones let go. I'm average at the job, not a star, and average is what gets cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomás the night it sinks in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're fine for a year whatever happens, because that's true, and that his job's safer than mine for once. Then I'd probably ask if he'd ever move somewhere cheaper. He'd say no, because his whole ward is here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the hands-on part lasts until robots come. Does that three years matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Showing a flat, checking a meter, handing over keys, that's maybe a third of my week. It buys time, but you don't need many people for that if the machine does everything else.

say: I'd say it's **far too fast** and the government should slow it down.
I'd share calls to keep **a real person** for tenants when things go wrong.
think: I think our firm shrinks to about **a third** of its staff within two years.
Only **viewings and handovers** stay human until around 2031, which is a thin lifeline.
do: Join the **agency staff union** in the first month.
Cancel the planned holiday and push savings towards **a full year**.
Apply for **housing officer** jobs with the council or a housing association.
feel: She feels **anxious**, seeing herself as **average** and so likely to be cut.
S2.quote: I'm average at the job, not a star, and average is what gets cut.
fieldNote: She names her own **average skill** as the reason she'd go, without self-pity.
Her plan moves her **towards public housing**, which fits her values.
The robot gap matters little because hands-on work is only **a third** of her week.

steps.text: Join the union for agency staff in the first month
Cancel the holiday and move the money into savings
Apply for council and housing association housing officer jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say we need rules, but I'd sound less panicked. At work I'd push for a plan on retraining, not just a memo. To friends I'd say five years is enough time to make it fair, if anyone bothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have about three good years in agency work before it really bites. That's enough to become lettings manager, but I'm not sure being manager of a branch run by software is much of a job. Privately, I'd start looking at the exit the moment it was announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the tenancy law course and then start a part-time housing management qualification, the sort housing associations ask for. I'd use the AI tools properly at work, because I'd want to know them inside out. I'd keep saving the same, since we're already in good shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. Five years feels like enough to land somewhere sensible. I'd still feel sad watching the branch thin out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a housing association rather than staying in sales or lettings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They aren't trying to squeeze the last pound out of every tenant. Housing associations will still need people to sit in someone's kitchen and sort out a repair. It's the part of my job I'm proudest of. I've done it a hundred times as a negotiator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tomás be part of that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because a housing association job probably pays less than what I get with commission. He'd say go for it. He's the one who's always telling me I like the tenants more than the landlords.

say: I'd push for a **retraining plan** at work, not just a memo.
I'd tell friends **five years** is enough to make this fair, if anyone tries.
think: I'd expect about **three good years** in agency work before it bites.
Being manager of a **software-run branch** doesn't sound like much of a job.
do: Finish the tenancy law course, then start a **housing management qualification**.
Learn the agency's **AI tools** properly while still employed.
Keep savings at the **current level**, which already feels enough.
feel: She feels **uneasy** rather than scared, and **sad** to watch the branch thin out.
S3.quote: Housing associations will still need people to sit in someone's kitchen and sort out a repair. It's the part of my job I'm proudest of.
fieldNote: Five years turns her exit from **a scramble** into a **planned move**.
She accepts a likely **pay cut** for work closer to her values.
She would learn AI tools more **when forced**, but not to stay in sales.

steps.text: Start a part-time housing management qualification in the first year
Learn the agency's AI lettings system inside out
Apply to housing associations once the qualification is underway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to get it right, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. At work I'd say we should be training people now, not in 2035. Online I'd be the annoying one sharing articles about rent controls and AI rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is most of my career so far times two. I'd be 37 when it arrives, which is young enough to switch and old enough to have something saved. I think it means I don't stay an estate agent forever, and maybe that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become lettings manager in the next few years, because that's still worth doing. I'd build the housing qualification slowly alongside it. And I'd probably talk to Tomás about buying a place now, while my job is solid and the mortgage people like my payslips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about myself, a little uneasy for everyone else. Ten years is a long runway. I worry more about Jodie and the older staff than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a place. Is that new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've been talking about it for a year. A decade's warning makes me want to lock in a home while we've got two good incomes. Renting at 37 with my job half gone sounds worse than renting now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in being worried about tenants and wanting to buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, but I've never said owning is bad. I just think renting shouldn't be miserable. If I can get out of renting, I'd still fight for the people who can't.

say: I'd say **a decade** leaves no excuse for anyone **left behind**.
I'd tell work we should start **training people now**, not in 2035.
think: I'd be **37** when it arrives, young enough to switch careers.
I probably **don't stay an agent** forever, and I can live with that.
do: Go for **lettings manager** in the next few years.
Build a **housing qualification** slowly alongside the job.
Talk to Tomás about **buying a home** while both incomes are solid.
feel: She feels **calm** about herself and **uneasy** for older colleagues.
S4.quote: Renting at 37 with my job half gone sounds worse than renting now.
fieldNote: The long runway shifts her focus to **locking in a home**.
She stays **progressive** but sees no clash with **owning**.
Her concern moves outward to **older colleagues** like Jodie.

steps.text: Apply for lettings manager when the next branch post opens
Study for a housing management qualification part-time
Look for a two-bed to buy with Tomás within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be one of the average ones cut before I'd had time to move. What would help is a proper retraining fund, paid for partly by the firms saving money, so people like Jodie and me can move into housing work without a big gap in pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. If AI runs lettings, I'd want a law that says a tenant can always reach a real person about repairs and deposits. Otherwise the cheapest system wins, and the cheapest system is never on the tenant's side.

headlineQuote: If AI runs lettings, I'd want a law that says a tenant can always reach a real person about repairs and deposits.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old lettings negotiator** at a city agency, with good pay and about nine months saved.
She cares most about **tenants**, and often feels she works for landlords she doesn't respect.
She picks up AI tools **once colleagues prove them**, and sees herself as solidly average.
Faster AGI pushes her **towards public housing** work, while a decade lets her buy a home first.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, when she'd be cut before she could move.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **retraining fund** paid partly by firms, and a right for tenants to reach a person.
